{"id":"ENG-2466","uuid":"5d929129-13be-4967-a32b-9fa707188f89","title":"Set sensible default privileges and explicit grants in migrations","description":"## Problem

* A database built from our migrations on Supabase image 17.11.0.018 (used for new preview branches) doesn't work for signed-in users. On the PR <pull-request id="26024a38-12f9-47da-9643-c0540d01de16" label="DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph#1609" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/review/eng-2459-remove-the-unused-pg-cron-and-pg-stat-monitor-extensions-a12e8a8653b6" /> preview branch, `authenticated` can't read `Concept`, `Content`, `Space` and 6 other tables, or 9 of the 11 views. It also can't execute functions that RLS policies call, such as `in_space` and `my_space_ids`.
* Our migrations don't set default privileges for tables, views or sequences, and most objects have no explicit `GRANT`. Privileges come from the image's defaults. Image 17.11.0.011 (local and production) gives `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` every privilege on new tables and sequences. Image 17.11.0.018 (preview branches) gives them only TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER and MAINTAIN on tables, and nothing on sequences or functions.
* Preview branches are unusable now, including for work in progress such as the `mira-collab` branch. Any other fresh build would be unusable too, and so would local builds if a CLI update brings the new image.
* The old defaults also leave every new table open to `anon` until its author revokes it, and give `anon` and `authenticated` TRUNCATE, which RLS doesn't limit.

## Solution

* Add a migration that sets our own default privileges in `public`, and grants every existing table, view, sequence and function explicitly to the roles that use it.

## Done When

* Explicit grants: a fresh build from migrations works on any Supabase image. On a preview branch, signed-in users can use the plugins as they do in production.
* Sensible defaults: a new object in `public` gives `anon` nothing. It gives `authenticated` SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on tables and views, USAGE on sequences and EXECUTE on functions, and gives `service_role` everything.
* Client roles hold only the privileges that clients use:
  * `anon` and `authenticated` have no TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES or MAINTAIN.
  * `my_groups`, `my_pseudo_accounts` and `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536` are read-only for them.
  * `anon` has only `SELECT` on `Space`, and can't execute functions that write, except `get_secret_token`.
* `security_model.md` describes the defaults, and says that a new table must enable RLS and a new view must run as the caller or filter by the caller.
* The schema files declare the same grants and default privileges as the migrations.

## Out of Scope

* Moving the `dbdiff` scripts to a new engine (<issue id="36144b5b-b165-42be-9f7c-903b073b5f8d" label="ENG-2461" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2461/move-the-dbdiff-scripts-off-the-deprecated-use-pg-schema-engine" />).
* A test that checks RLS and client privileges on every object in `public`. See the issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY>)

## Notes

* Production keeps its existing grants, so the migration mostly makes them explicit there. Its default privileges change too: check that nothing in production creates objects that rely on the old defaults.
* `Space`: `create-space` reads it with the caller's key, so `anon` keeps `SELECT`. Its writes use the service key. Confirm that no other client inserts into `Space` without a login.
* `anon` keeps EXECUTE on the read-only functions it has today. Some of them will be used by <issue id="dedef7aa-ec23-4eb0-b9e2-de0e5ceeb900" label="ENG-1837" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1837/add-a-public-status-in-the-database" />, so trimming them waits.
* Evidence and the comparison with production: Roam issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C>). It also absorbs the TRUNCATE candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9>).
* Until this is fixed, don't update the local Supabase CLI. A newer version may bring the new image.

I've updated ENG-2466's Done When to match your decisions. It now covers:
- **Explicit grants:** a fresh build works on any image.
- **The new defaults:** `anon` gets nothing; `authenticated` gets SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on tables and views, USAGE on sequences and EXECUTE on functions; `service_role` gets everything.

- **`security_model.md`,** which must state the rules for RLS and views.
- **The schema files,** which must declare the same grants as the migrations.

Notes has the new line you asked for: "`anon` keeps EXECUTE on the read-only functions it has today. Some of them will be used by ENG-1837, so trimming them waits."

1. **One new migration.** It sets the new default privileges, explicitly grants every existing object what production has today, then applies the reductions.
2. **The same grants and defaults in the schema files.** This includes replacing `base.sql`'s current `GRANT ALL … TO anon` defaults.
3. **`security_model.md`,** with the defaults and the rules for RLS and views.
4. **`functionGrants.feature`:** the six trimmed functions get permission-error checks for `anon`.

To check the work, I'd rerun the inventory on a reset local database and diff it against production. The only differences should be the intended reductions. Then I'd ask you before running cucumber.

Should I start on step 1?

{"id":"ENG-2466","uuid":"5d929129-13be-4967-a32b-9fa707188f89","title":"Set sensible default privileges and explicit grants in migrations","description":"## Problem

* A database built from our migrations on Supabase image 17.11.0.018 (used for new preview branches) doesn't work for signed-in users. On the PR <pull-request id="26024a38-12f9-47da-9643-c0540d01de16" label="DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph#1609" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/review/eng-2459-remove-the-unused-pg-cron-and-pg-stat-monitor-extensions-a12e8a8653b6" /> preview branch, `authenticated` can't read `Concept`, `Content`, `Space` and 6 other tables, or 9 of the 11 views. It also can't execute functions that RLS policies call, such as `in_space` and `my_space_ids`.
* Our migrations don't set default privileges for tables, views or sequences, and most objects have no explicit `GRANT`. Privileges come from the image's defaults. Image 17.11.0.011 (local and production) gives `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` every privilege on new tables and sequences. Image 17.11.0.018 (preview branches) gives them only TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER and MAINTAIN on tables, and nothing on sequences or functions.
* Preview branches are unusable now, including for work in progress such as the `mira-collab` branch. Any other fresh build would be unusable too, and so would local builds if a CLI update brings the new image.
* The old defaults also leave every new table open to `anon` until its author revokes it, and give `anon` and `authenticated` TRUNCATE, which RLS doesn't limit.

## Solution

* Add a migration that sets our own default privileges in `public`, and grants every existing table, view, sequence and function explicitly to the roles that use it.

## Done When

* Explicit grants: a fresh build from migrations works on any Supabase image. On a preview branch, signed-in users can use the plugins as they do in production.
* Sensible defaults: a new object in `public` gives `anon` nothing. It gives `authenticated` SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on tables and views, USAGE on sequences and EXECUTE on functions, and gives `service_role` everything.
* Client roles hold only the privileges that clients use:
  * `anon` and `authenticated` have no TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES or MAINTAIN.
  * `my_groups`, `my_pseudo_accounts` and `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536` are read-only for them.
  * On `Space`, `anon` keeps `SELECT` and loses its other privileges.
  * `anon` can't execute functions that write, except `get_secret_token`.
* `security_model.md` describes the defaults, and says that a new table must enable RLS and a new view must run as the caller or filter by the caller.
* The schema files declare the same grants and default privileges as the migrations.

## Out of Scope

* Moving the `dbdiff` scripts to a new engine (<issue id="36144b5b-b165-42be-9f7c-903b073b5f8d" label="ENG-2461" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2461/move-the-dbdiff-scripts-off-the-deprecated-use-pg-schema-engine" />).
* A test that checks RLS and client privileges on every object in `public`. See the issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY>)

## Notes

* Production keeps its existing grants, so the migration mostly makes them explicit there. Its default privileges change too: check that nothing in production creates objects that rely on the old defaults.
* `Space`: `create-space` reads it with the caller's key, so `anon` keeps `SELECT`. Its writes use the service key. Confirm that no other client inserts into `Space` without a login.
* `anon` keeps EXECUTE on the read-only functions it has today. Some of them will be used by <issue id="dedef7aa-ec23-4eb0-b9e2-de0e5ceeb900" label="ENG-1837" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1837/add-a-public-status-in-the-database" />, so trimming them waits.
* Evidence and the comparison with production: Roam issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C>). It also absorbs the TRUNCATE candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9>).
* Until this is fixed, don't update the local Supabase CLI. A newer version may bring the new image.

content.text:
Both facts matter for the design:
- **`REVOKE ALL ON TABLE` also removes column grants.** All 18 column grants on `PlatformAccount` disappeared. So any reset has to grant them again.
- **`GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA` includes views.**

Here's the design I'd use. **Why it matters:** it decides whether the schema files list every privilege of every object, or only the exceptions.

**Defaults plus exceptions:**
1. **Migration, step 1: our own defaults.** `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public`: revoke everything from `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role`, then grant the defaults you chose. On .018 this also removes the TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES and MAINTAIN that the image gives clients.
2. **Migration, step 2: reset every existing object to those defaults,** whatever image built it. `REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES/SEQUENCES/FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public` from the client roles and PUBLIC, then grant the default privileges with `ON ALL … IN SCHEMA`.
3. **Migration, step 3: the exceptions, object by object.** These are listed below.
4. **Schema files:** `base.sql` declares the new defaults. Each object's file then declares only its exceptions, and the redundant `GRANT ALL … TO authenticated/service_role` lines go, since the defaults now cover them. A reader sees what's special about each object, not 356 lines of routine grants.

The exceptions, from the inventory:
- **`anon`:**
  - `SELECT` on `Space`, `concept_contributors`, `content_contributors` and all 11 views.
  - EXECUTE on the 34 read-only functions and `get_secret_token`.
- **`authenticated`, granted less than the default:**
  - `PlatformAccount`: column grants only, as today.
  - `file_gc`: nothing.
  - The 11 views: `SELECT` only.
  - The 9 functions only triggers use: no EXECUTE.
- **`service_role`:** `SELECT` only on `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` and `my_resource_grants`, as today.

The alternative is to list every grant of every object, in the migration and in the schema files. That's more explicit but much longer, and it would hide the exceptions among the routine grants.

One small point not in Done When: on the 2 sequences, `authenticated` holds `SELECT, UPDATE, USAGE` today. The new default gives only `USAGE`, which is all that inserting a row needs (`nextval`). To keep "same as production apart from the reductions", I'd grant those two existing sequences `SELECT, UPDATE, USAGE` explicitly. Or should `USAGE` alone be enough here too?

Does this design suit you?

{"id":"ENG-2466","uuid":"5d929129-13be-4967-a32b-9fa707188f89","title":"Set sensible default privileges and explicit grants in migrations","description":"## Problem

* A database built from our migrations on Supabase image 17.11.0.018 (used for new preview branches) doesn't work for signed-in users. On the PR <pull-request id="26024a38-12f9-47da-9643-c0540d01de16" label="DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph#1609" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/review/eng-2459-remove-the-unused-pg-cron-and-pg-stat-monitor-extensions-a12e8a8653b6" /> preview branch, `authenticated` can't read `Concept`, `Content`, `Space` and 6 other tables, or 9 of the 11 views. It also can't execute functions that RLS policies call, such as `in_space` and `my_space_ids`.
* Our migrations don't set default privileges for tables, views or sequences, and most objects have no explicit `GRANT`. Privileges come from the image's defaults. Image 17.11.0.011 (local and production) gives `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` every privilege on new tables and sequences. Image 17.11.0.018 (preview branches) gives them only TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER and MAINTAIN on tables, and nothing on sequences or functions.
* Preview branches are unusable now, including for work in progress such as the `mira-collab` branch. Any other fresh build would be unusable too, and so would local builds if a CLI update brings the new image.
* The old defaults also leave every new table open to `anon` until its author revokes it, and give `anon` and `authenticated` TRUNCATE, which RLS doesn't limit.

## Solution

* Add a migration that sets our own default privileges in `public`, and grants every existing table, view, sequence and function explicitly to the roles that use it.

## Done When

* Explicit grants: a fresh build from migrations works on any Supabase image. On a preview branch, signed-in users can use the plugins as they do in production.
* Sensible defaults: a new object in `public` gives `anon` nothing. It gives `authenticated` SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on tables and views, USAGE and SELECT on sequences, and EXECUTE on functions, and gives `service_role` everything.
* Client roles hold only the privileges that clients use:
  * `anon` and `authenticated` have no TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES or MAINTAIN.
  * `my_groups`, `my_pseudo_accounts` and `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536` are read-only for them.
  * On `Space`, `anon` keeps `SELECT` and loses its other privileges.
  * `anon` can't execute functions that write, except `get_secret_token`, needed for web handoff.
* `security_model.md` describes the defaults, and says that a new table must enable RLS and a new view must run as the caller or filter by the caller.
* The schema files declare the same grants and default privileges as the migrations.

## Out of Scope

* Moving the `dbdiff` scripts to a new engine (<issue id="36144b5b-b165-42be-9f7c-903b073b5f8d" label="ENG-2461" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2461/move-the-dbdiff-scripts-off-the-deprecated-use-pg-schema-engine" />).
* A test that checks RLS and client privileges on every object in `public`. See the issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/BzGAwTpZY>)

## Notes

* Production keeps its existing grants, so the migration mostly makes them explicit there. Its default privileges change too: check that nothing in production creates objects that rely on the old defaults.
* `Space`: `create-space` reads it with the caller's key, so `anon` keeps `SELECT`. Its writes use the service key. Confirm that no other client inserts into `Space` without a login.
* `anon` keeps EXECUTE on the read-only functions it has today. Some of them will be used by <issue id="dedef7aa-ec23-4eb0-b9e2-de0e5ceeb900" label="ENG-1837" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1837/add-a-public-status-in-the-database" />, so trimming them waits.
* Evidence and the comparison with production: Roam issue candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/F6tFBTx5C>). It also absorbs the TRUNCATE candidate [https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/E9_NZrWH9>).
* Until this is fixed, don't update the local Supabase CLI. A newer version may bring the new image.

message.content: nit: Why are the anon table and view grants separate?

content.text:
There's no strong reason. I grouped the statements by why `anon` needs them:
- **The three tables each have their own reason.** `Space` is there because `create-space` reads it to check the caller's key; the contributor tables because public reads join them.
- **The views get `SELECT` across the board,** because the views are the read API. That's also why the `anon` view grant sits next to the revoke that makes the views read-only for `authenticated`.

But the form isn't consistent: three separate statements for the tables, one combined statement for the views. And the comment above the tables gives a reason only for `Space`. I'd make it one `GRANT SELECT … TO anon` for the three tables, with a comment giving each table's reason. The views would stay with the read-only block. Alternatively, all 14 objects could go in a single statement. That's shorter, but the reasons would be harder to read.

Which do you prefer?

#!/bin/bash
S=$1; SCH=$2

  { echo "BEGIN;"; echo "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE;"; echo "CREATE SCHEMA public AUTHORIZATION pg_database_owner;"; cat $S/defaults_$mode.sql;

  grep -P "^(function|table|view|sequence)\t" $S/schema_$mode.raw > $S/schema_$mode.tsv
  echo "$mode: $(wc -l < $S/schema_$mode.tsv) rows"
  if diff <(LC_ALL=C sort $S/privileges_expected.tsv) <(LC_ALL=C sort $S/schema_$mode.tsv) > $S/schema_$mode.diff; then echo "$mode: SCHEMA FILES MATCH EXPECTED"; else head -30 $S/schema_$mode.diff; fi
done
EOF

53:They are not `security_invoker`: they run as their owner, bypass RLS, and apply their own access filter. The views compute the user's accessible spaces once per query, in the InitPlan form above (ENG-2344, ENG-2359).

60:- Single-table views are automatically updatable, and writes through them would also bypass RLS. Write privileges are revoked on `my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents` and `my_file_references` (ENG-2368, ENG-2359). Any new updatable view needs the same `REVOKE`.

102:`anon` will read public nodes, their files and their authors (ENG-1837). 132:- New table: enable RLS, write policies for each operation, and revoke `anon` unless anonymous readers need it. Add visibility scenarios to `features/`, like `features/conceptAccess.feature`.

137:- New trigger function: revoke it from `anon` and `authenticated`.
139:- New definer view: `REVOKE ALL` and then `GRANT SELECT`, because default privileges give write privileges. Set `security_barrier`, and return only what every caller may already see, including through row counts.
151:- ENG-2442: function grants made explicit, and new functions no longer executable by `anon`.

content.content:
1	# Database access control
2	
3	This note explains how the database decides who can read and write what, why some of its choices look risky to Supabase's security advisor, and the rules a change must follow to keep access correct. Read it before adding a table, a policy, a view or a `SECURITY DEFINER` function. Update it when one of those rules changes.
4	
5	## Roles
6	
7	Supabase sends every API request as one of three Postgres roles:
8	
9	- `anon`: a request made with the public API key and no login.
10	- `authenticated`: a logged-in request. The plugins log in as their space's "anonymous" account (`agent_type = 'anonymous'`), so they use `authenticated`, not `anon`.
11	- `service_role`: the server key. It bypasses row-level security. Edge functions such as `create-space` use it; clients never get it.
12	
13	`anon` reads almost nothing today.
14	
15	## How access is enforced
16	
17	Every table has row-level security (RLS) policies. Postgres checks them for each row a query touches.
18	
19	The policies call helper functions such as `my_space_ids(access_level)` and `account_ids_in_shared_spaces(access_level)`. Most helpers are `SECURITY DEFINER` with `SET search_path = ''`: they run with the owner's rights, so they can read `SpaceAccess` and `group_membership` without being filtered by those tables' policies, and a policy calling them doesn't recurse into other policies.
20	
21	The `SET` clause stops Postgres from inlining a helper, so a helper that takes a row column runs its own query for every row. Policies avoid this by calling helpers that take no row column, wrapped in `(SELECT ...)`, for example `space_id = any((SELECT my_space_ids('reader'))::bigint [])`. Postgres evaluates that form, an InitPlan, once per query (ENG-2443, ENG-2446). The policies on the contributor tables' writes, `group_membership` and `sync_info` still call a helper per row.
22	
23	`my_user_accounts()` is the base of most helpers. It returns the current user's id and the ids of the groups they belong to. A space or resource is accessible when a `SpaceAccess` or `ResourceAccess` row grants it to one of those ids. It is declared `ROWS 10`, because Postgres can't inline it and its default estimate of 1000 rows makes the planner scan `SpaceAccess`. The hint changes only the plan, not who sees what.
24	
25	### Policies that read `LocalAccess`
26	
27	The `AgentIdentifier` select policy and the `PlatformAccount` write policies read `LocalAccess` directly, through its primary key, so checking one account stays cheap. They read it as the caller, so its own select policy filters what they see: narrowing `local_access_select_policy` narrows them too, with no error.
28	
29	That filter starts at `reader`, but `PlatformAccount` rows are visible from `partial`. So the `PlatformAccount` select policy reads the definer view `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` instead. Unlike a function, Postgres can inline a view, so one account is checked per row through the primary key, and a full read builds its set once. Three things about this view must stay:
30	
31	- `DISTINCT`, and no `space_id` column. One row per membership would reveal memberships that `LocalAccess` hides below `reader`.
32	- `security_barrier`. Without it, a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access join and see accounts from other spaces.
33	- Its grants: `SELECT` only. `anon` holds it for public access (see [Grants made for public access](#grants-made-for-public-access)). It returns no rows to `anon` today.
34	
35	### Account and group writes
36	
37	- `authenticated` can't insert into `PlatformAccount`, and has `UPDATE` on it per column, so clients can't set who owns an account (`dg_account`) or change what identifies it (`agent_type`, `platform`, `account_local_id`). A new column isn't client-writable until it's added to the grant. Clients create and upsert accounts through `upsert_account_in_space`, which also adds the account to the space (ENG-2447).
38	- `upsert_account_in_space` requires editor access to the space, and grants no `SpaceAccess` (ENG-2439). `LocalAccess` says an account belongs to a space and grants nothing.
39	- `LocalAccess` writes require editor access to the row's own space (ENG-2447).
40	- Only a group's admins can add members. The `create-group` edge function adds the first admin with the service role, and `accept_group_invitation` adds invited members (ENG-2438).
41	
42	### Account reads
43	
44	- `authenticated` has `SELECT` on `PlatformAccount` per column, without `dg_account` and `metadata`, and `my_accounts` leaves out both columns too (ENG-2441). `dg_account` would show which accounts belong to one person, and nothing uses `metadata` yet.
45	- A column grant applies to every row, so clients can't read their own `dg_account` from the table either. They get their own user id from their session, and their own accounts from `my_platform_account_ids`.
46	- Clients must name the columns they read from `PlatformAccount`. `select("*")`, and any filter on a hidden column, fails with a permission error.
47	- `my_pseudo_accounts` returns `dg_account`, so it has to stay a definer view. Any `anon` grant on `PlatformAccount` has to use the same column list.
48	
49	### The `my_*` views
50	
51	The `my_*` views (`my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents`, `my_file_references`, `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536`, `my_pseudo_accounts`, `my_groups`) are the main way clients read data.
52	
53	They are not `security_invoker`: they run as their owner, bypass RLS, and apply their own access filter. This was done for speed, when policies called their helpers once per row and large reads timed out (ENG-1433, ENG-1435). The views compute the user's accessible spaces once per query, in the InitPlan form above (ENG-2344, ENG-2359).
54	
55	The policies now use that form too, but most views stay definer, because they're still faster. Under RLS, a filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` has to run after the policy, so it can't use an index. `concept_in_relations` filters with `@>`, and took about 250 times as long through RLS with 273 `ResourceAccess` rows. Reading the tables directly has the same cost. So by default, clients read through these views and write to the tables. The timings are on ENG-2444, which is parked.
56	
57	Consequences:
58	
59	- Each view's filter is a second copy of the table's access rules. A change to a policy must be repeated in the views that read the table. We accept this cost, and the security advisor keeps reporting these views.
60	- Single-table views are automatically updatable, and writes through them would also bypass RLS. Write privileges are revoked on `my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents` and `my_file_references` (ENG-2368, ENG-2359). Any new updatable view needs the same `REVOKE`.
61	- Clients depend on the view names and columns, including older plugin versions that are still installed, PostgREST's foreign-key inference and the generated types. Keep them stable.
62	- They have no `security_barrier`, so a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access filter and see rows the view would hide (measured on `my_accounts`). PostgREST's fixed filter operators shouldn't allow such a filter, so this matters for direct SQL access. The same reordering is what lets `@>` use its index, so time the relation queries before adding `security_barrier` to `my_concepts`.
63	
64	## Function grants
65	
66	A new function in `public` is executable by `authenticated` and `service_role`, not by `anon`. `base.sql` sets this with default privileges, in two parts:
67	
68	- It revokes `anon` from the `public` schema's defaults, which Supabase sets up to include it.
69	- It revokes `PUBLIC` from the global defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it, so the first part alone changes nothing. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.
70	
71	Every `anon` grant and every revoke is explicit, next to the function in its schema file, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs it. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file.
72	
73	`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too.
74	
75	### Rules
76	
77	1. A function or view used by a policy must be usable by every role that queries that table: EXECUTE on the function, SELECT on the view. Without it, the query fails with a permission error; it does not return zero rows.
78	2. Functions called in a view are checked against the role querying the view, not the view owner. A function that is not `SECURITY DEFINER` also runs its body as that role, under the policies of whatever it reads. For example, the views call `my_accessible_resources()`, which reads `ResourceAccess` as the caller.
79	3. Trigger functions need no grant. Postgres checks EXECUTE when the trigger is created, not when it fires.
80	4. A `SECURITY DEFINER` function that clients can call must check the caller's access itself, because it skips RLS. Don't rely on capping a permission with `least(...)`: `LEAST` ignores NULL, so a caller with no access (NULL) gets the other argument.
81	5. A helper that clients can call may reveal only facts about the caller, facts about resources the caller can read, or facts about identities whose owner made them public.
82	
83	One helper doesn't follow rule 5 yet. `file_exists` says whether any space holds a file with a given hash; the caller must already know the hash.
84	
85	### Functions `anon` can execute
86	
87	| Function           | Why                                                                                                                                                                                      |
88	| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
89	| `get_secret_token` | The website's `/auth/token` route, which hands a plugin's session to a browser that isn't logged in yet. The token is 12 random bytes, single use, with a 45-second expiry for this flow |
90	| `my_user_accounts` | Public access: base of the views and helpers                                                                                                                                             |
91	| `my_space_ids`     | `Space` select policy; `anon` can read `Space`. Public access: the `my_*` views and the other select policies                                                                            |
92	| `file_access`      | Public access: the storage read policy on the `assets` bucket                                                                                                                            |
93	
94	All other `SECURITY DEFINER` functions are executable by `authenticated` only. Trigger functions, and `is_last_local_reference` (which only triggers call), are executable by neither role.
95	
96	`in_space` is not executable by `anon`. Only write paths reach it as the caller, and `anon`'s reads use `my_space_ids`.
97	
98	`anon` holds only `SELECT` on the contributor tables, and its reads fail with a permission error on `ResourceAccess` until public access adds the grants below.
99	
100	### Grants made for public access
101	
102	`anon` will read public nodes, their files and their authors (ENG-1837). The "Public access" entries above, and `anon`'s `SELECT` on `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces`, `my_resource_grants` and the contributor tables, are grants made ahead of that work. Keep them: rule 1 means that removing one fails those queries with a permission error. ENG-1837 also has to grant `anon` `SELECT` on `Concept`, `Content`, `Document`, `FileReference` and `ResourceAccess`, and open `storage_select_assets_access` to `anon`, which today applies only to `authenticated`.
103	
104	## Supabase advisor findings that remain
105	
106	Supabase runs two advisors on the database, one for security and one for performance. Both check shapes, not behaviour, so some of their findings are expected and stay.
107	
108	### Security advisor
109	
110	It flags any view that bypasses RLS, any view that reads `auth.users`, any policy whose condition is always true, and any `SECURITY DEFINER` function a client role can execute. It can't tell whether a function or view leaks anything. These findings are expected:
111	
112	- `my_groups` reads `auth.users` (`auth_users_exposed` and `security_definer_view`). Groups are rows in `auth.users`, with the synthetic email `{group name}@groups.discoursegraphs.com` set by the `create-group` edge function. The view returns only the id and name of the groups the current user belongs to; `anon` gets no rows. It must run as its owner, because clients can't read `auth.users`. This stays.
113	- The other eight `my_*` views (`security_definer_view`). This is the speed workaround described above.
114	- `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` (`security_definer_view`). It runs as its owner on purpose, to read `LocalAccess` below `reader` (see above). It stays.
115	- `anon_security_definer_function_executable` for the four functions in the table above.
116	- `authenticated_security_definer_function_executable` for the policy helpers and for the functions that clients call directly: `create_account_in_space`, `upsert_accounts_in_space`, `file_exists`, `create_secret_token`, `get_secret_token`, `accept_group_invitation`. Also for `upsert_account_in_space`: no client calls it, but `upsert_content` and `upsert_documents` run as the caller, so the caller needs `EXECUTE`.
117	- `space_insert_policy` on `Space` (`rls_policy_always_true`). The insert policy is `WITH CHECK (true)`, but no client relies on it: `create-space` creates spaces with the service role. Whether to remove it is still open. Reading, changing and deleting a space still require access to it: those policies check `my_space_ids`.
118	
119	### Performance advisor
120	
121	These findings are expected:
122	
123	- `FileReference_content_fkey` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). Deleting a `Content` row looks up its `FileReference` rows through the primary key `(source_local_id, space_id, filepath)`. The advisor flags it only because the key's column order differs from the foreign key's.
124	- The foreign keys from `AgentIdentifier.account_id`, `LocalAccess.space_id`, `SpaceAccess.space_id`, `concept_contributors.contributor_id` and `content_contributors.contributor_id` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). Only deleting an account or a space would use an index on them, and both are rare. Revisit if either becomes routine.
125	- The foreign keys from `Concept.author_id`, `Content.author_id`, `Content.creator_id` and `Document.author_id` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). An index would help account deletion and queries by author, neither of which is in use yet, and every sync insert would pay for it. Decide when the first feature that needs one is planned, measured against its queries. A composite index such as `(space_id, author_id)` may fit better, since reads are already scoped to a list of spaces.
126	- `Content_text` (`unused_index`). Kept for database searches on content text, which are planned but not yet used.
127	
128	Any other finding from either advisor is new, and should be fixed or added here with its reason.
129	
130	## Checklist for changes
131	
132	- New table: enable RLS, write policies for each operation, and revoke `anon` unless anonymous readers need it. Add visibility scenarios to `features/`, like `features/conceptAccess.feature`.
133	- New policy: wrap calls that don't depend on the row in `(SELECT ...)`. Write `(SELECT auth.uid())`, not `auth.uid()`. Don't pass a row column to a helper that sets `search_path`. If the policy reads another table directly, remember that table's own select policy filters what it sees.
134	- New `PlatformAccount` column: decide whether clients may read or write it, and add it to the per-column grants if so.
135	- New `SECURITY DEFINER` function: set `search_path = ''`, check the caller's access inside it (rule 4), grant it only to the roles that call it, and add a comment saying who that is.
136	- New function that `anon` reaches, directly, through a policy or through a view: grant it to `anon` in its schema file and in the migration.
137	- New trigger function: revoke it from `anon` and `authenticated`.
138	- New or changed view: keep existing names and columns, mirror the table's access rules, and revoke write privileges if the view is updatable.
139	- New definer view: `REVOKE ALL` and then `GRANT SELECT`, because default privileges give write privileges. Set `security_barrier`, and return only what every caller may already see, including through row counts.
140	- Before merging, run the cucumber suite and compare both Supabase advisors' lists with the findings above.
141	
142	## History
143	
144	- ENG-950, ENG-1433, ENG-1435: the `my_*` views, introduced to avoid per-row policy costs.
145	- ENG-2344, ENG-2359: the views rewritten with InitPlans.
146	- ENG-2368: write privileges revoked on the updatable views.
147	- ENG-1480, ENG-2436: Supabase findings reviewed and documented.
148	- ENG-2438: joining a group limited to its admins, and `group_exists` removed.
149	- ENG-2439: `upsert_account_in_space` requires editor access and grants no `SpaceAccess`.
150	- ENG-2441: `dg_account` and `metadata` removed from `my_accounts` and hidden on `PlatformAccount`.
151	- ENG-2442: function grants made explicit, and new functions no longer executable by `anon`.
152	- ENG-2443, ENG-2446: policies moved to the InitPlan form, and `can_access_account`, `can_view_concept`, `can_view_content`, `account_in_shared_space`, `unowned_account_in_shared_space` and `is_my_account` removed.
153	- ENG-2447: account columns granted individually, and `LocalAccess` writes checked against the row's space.
154	- ENG-2448: the unused `access_token` table removed.

# Database access control

This note explains how the database decides who can read and write what, why some of its choices look risky to Supabase's security advisor, and the rules a change must follow to keep access correct. Read it before adding a table, a policy, a view or a `SECURITY DEFINER` function. Update it when one of those rules changes.

## Roles

Supabase sends every API request as one of three Postgres roles:

- `anon`: a request made with the public API key and no login.
- `authenticated`: a logged-in request. The plugins log in as their space's "anonymous" account (`agent_type = 'anonymous'`), so they use `authenticated`, not `anon`.
- `service_role`: the server key. It bypasses row-level security. Edge functions such as `create-space` use it; clients never get it.

`anon` reads almost nothing today.

## How access is enforced

Every table has row-level security (RLS) policies. Postgres checks them for each row a query touches.

The policies call helper functions such as `my_space_ids(access_level)` and `account_ids_in_shared_spaces(access_level)`. Most helpers are `SECURITY DEFINER` with `SET search_path = ''`: they run with the owner's rights, so they can read `SpaceAccess` and `group_membership` without being filtered by those tables' policies, and a policy calling them doesn't recurse into other policies.

The `SET` clause stops Postgres from inlining a helper, so a helper that takes a row column runs its own query for every row. Policies avoid this by calling helpers that take no row column, wrapped in `(SELECT ...)`, for example `space_id = any((SELECT my_space_ids('reader'))::bigint [])`. Postgres evaluates that form, an InitPlan, once per query (ENG-2443, ENG-2446). The policies on the contributor tables' writes, `group_membership` and `sync_info` still call a helper per row.

`my_user_accounts()` is the base of most helpers. It returns the current user's id and the ids of the groups they belong to. A space or resource is accessible when a `SpaceAccess` or `ResourceAccess` row grants it to one of those ids. It is declared `ROWS 10`, because Postgres can't inline it and its default estimate of 1000 rows makes the planner scan `SpaceAccess`. The hint changes only the plan, not who sees what.

### Policies that read `LocalAccess`

The `AgentIdentifier` select policy and the `PlatformAccount` write policies read `LocalAccess` directly, through its primary key, so checking one account stays cheap. They read it as the caller, so its own select policy filters what they see: narrowing `local_access_select_policy` narrows them too, with no error.

That filter starts at `reader`, but `PlatformAccount` rows are visible from `partial`. So the `PlatformAccount` select policy reads the definer view `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` instead. Unlike a function, Postgres can inline a view, so one account is checked per row through the primary key, and a full read builds its set once. Three things about this view must stay:

- `DISTINCT`, and no `space_id` column. One row per membership would reveal memberships that `LocalAccess` hides below `reader`.
- `security_barrier`. Without it, a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access join and see accounts from other spaces.
- Its grants: `SELECT` only. `anon` holds it for public access (see [Grants made for public access](#grants-made-for-public-access)). It returns no rows to `anon` today.

### Account and group writes

- `authenticated` can't insert into `PlatformAccount`, and has `UPDATE` on it per column, so clients can't set who owns an account (`dg_account`) or change what identifies it (`agent_type`, `platform`, `account_local_id`). A new column isn't client-writable until it's added to the grant. Clients create and upsert accounts through `upsert_account_in_space`, which also adds the account to the space (ENG-2447).
- `upsert_account_in_space` requires editor access to the space, and grants no `SpaceAccess` (ENG-2439). `LocalAccess` says an account belongs to a space and grants nothing.
- `LocalAccess` writes require editor access to the row's own space (ENG-2447).
- Only a group's admins can add members. The `create-group` edge function adds the first admin with the service role, and `accept_group_invitation` adds invited members (ENG-2438).

### Account reads

- `authenticated` has `SELECT` on `PlatformAccount` per column, without `dg_account` and `metadata`, and `my_accounts` leaves out both columns too (ENG-2441). `dg_account` would show which accounts belong to one person, and nothing uses `metadata` yet.
- A column grant applies to every row, so clients can't read their own `dg_account` from the table either. They get their own user id from their session, and their own accounts from `my_platform_account_ids`.
- Clients must name the columns they read from `PlatformAccount`. `select("*")`, and any filter on a hidden column, fails with a permission error.
- `my_pseudo_accounts` returns `dg_account`, so it has to stay a definer view. Any `anon` grant on `PlatformAccount` has to use the same column list.

### The `my_*` views

The `my_*` views (`my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents`, `my_file_references`, `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536`, `my_pseudo_accounts`, `my_groups`) are the main way clients read data.

They are not `security_invoker`: they run as their owner, bypass RLS, and apply their own access filter. This was done for speed, when policies called their helpers once per row and large reads timed out (ENG-1433, ENG-1435). The views compute the user's accessible spaces once per query, in the InitPlan form above (ENG-2344, ENG-2359).

The policies now use that form too, but most views stay definer, because they're still faster. Under RLS, a filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` has to run after the policy, so it can't use an index. `concept_in_relations` filters with `@>`, and took about 250 times as long through RLS with 273 `ResourceAccess` rows. Reading the tables directly has the same cost. So by default, clients read through these views and write to the tables. The timings are on ENG-2444, which is parked.

Consequences:

- Each view's filter is a second copy of the table's access rules. A change to a policy must be repeated in the views that read the table. We accept this cost, and the security advisor keeps reporting these views.
- Single-table views are automatically updatable, and writes through them would also bypass RLS. Write privileges are revoked on `my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents` and `my_file_references` (ENG-2368, ENG-2359). Any new updatable view needs the same `REVOKE`.
- Clients depend on the view names and columns, including older plugin versions that are still installed, PostgREST's foreign-key inference and the generated types. Keep them stable.
- They have no `security_barrier`, so a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access filter and see rows the view would hide (measured on `my_accounts`). PostgREST's fixed filter operators shouldn't allow such a filter, so this matters for direct SQL access. The same reordering is what lets `@>` use its index, so time the relation queries before adding `security_barrier` to `my_concepts`.

## Function grants

A new function in `public` is executable by `authenticated` and `service_role`, not by `anon`. `base.sql` sets this with default privileges, in two parts:

- It revokes `anon` from the `public` schema's defaults, which Supabase sets up to include it.
- It revokes `PUBLIC` from the global defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it, so the first part alone changes nothing. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

Every `anon` grant and every revoke is explicit, next to the function in its schema file, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs it. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too.

### Rules

1. A function or view used by a policy must be usable by every role that queries that table: EXECUTE on the function, SELECT on the view. Without it, the query fails with a permission error; it does not return zero rows.
2. Functions called in a view are checked against the role querying the view, not the view owner. A function that is not `SECURITY DEFINER` also runs its body as that role, under the policies of whatever it reads. For example, the views call `my_accessible_resources()`, which reads `ResourceAccess` as the caller.
3. Trigger functions need no grant. Postgres checks EXECUTE when the trigger is created, not when it fires.
4. A `SECURITY DEFINER` function that clients can call must check the caller's access itself, because it skips RLS. Don't rely on capping a permission with `least(...)`: `LEAST` ignores NULL, so a caller with no access (NULL) gets the other argument.
5. A helper that clients can call may reveal only facts about the caller, facts about resources the caller can read, or facts about identities whose owner made them public.

One helper doesn't follow rule 5 yet. `file_exists` says whether any space holds a file with a given hash; the caller must already know the hash.

### Functions `anon` can execute

| Function           | Why                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `get_secret_token` | The website's `/auth/token` route, which hands a plugin's session to a browser that isn't logged in yet. The token is 12 random bytes, single use, with a 45-second expiry for this flow |
| `my_user_accounts` | Public access: base of the views and helpers                                                                                                                                             |
| `my_space_ids`     | `Space` select policy; `anon` can read `Space`. Public access: the `my_*` views and the other select policies                                                                            |
| `file_access`      | Public access: the storage read policy on the `assets` bucket                                                                                                                            |

All other `SECURITY DEFINER` functions are executable by `authenticated` only. Trigger functions, and `is_last_local_reference` (which only triggers call), are executable by neither role.

`in_space` is not executable by `anon`. Only write paths reach it as the caller, and `anon`'s reads use `my_space_ids`.

`anon` holds only `SELECT` on the contributor tables, and its reads fail with a permission error on `ResourceAccess` until public access adds the grants below.

### Grants made for public access

`anon` will read public nodes, their files and their authors (ENG-1837). The "Public access" entries above, and `anon`'s `SELECT` on `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces`, `my_resource_grants` and the contributor tables, are grants made ahead of that work. Keep them: rule 1 means that removing one fails those queries with a permission error. ENG-1837 also has to grant `anon` `SELECT` on `Concept`, `Content`, `Document`, `FileReference` and `ResourceAccess`, and open `storage_select_assets_access` to `anon`, which today applies only to `authenticated`.

## Supabase advisor findings that remain

Supabase runs two advisors on the database, one for security and one for performance. Both check shapes, not behaviour, so some of their findings are expected and stay.

### Security advisor

It flags any view that bypasses RLS, any view that reads `auth.users`, any policy whose condition is always true, and any `SECURITY DEFINER` function a client role can execute. It can't tell whether a function or view leaks anything. These findings are expected:

- `my_groups` reads `auth.users` (`auth_users_exposed` and `security_definer_view`). Groups are rows in `auth.users`, with the synthetic email `{group name}@groups.discoursegraphs.com` set by the `create-group` edge function. The view returns only the id and name of the groups the current user belongs to; `anon` gets no rows. It must run as its owner, because clients can't read `auth.users`. This stays.
- The other eight `my_*` views (`security_definer_view`). This is the speed workaround described above.
- `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` (`security_definer_view`). It runs as its owner on purpose, to read `LocalAccess` below `reader` (see above). It stays.
- `anon_security_definer_function_executable` for the four functions in the table above.
- `authenticated_security_definer_function_executable` for the policy helpers and for the functions that clients call directly: `create_account_in_space`, `upsert_accounts_in_space`, `file_exists`, `create_secret_token`, `get_secret_token`, `accept_group_invitation`. Also for `upsert_account_in_space`: no client calls it, but `upsert_content` and `upsert_documents` run as the caller, so the caller needs `EXECUTE`.
- `space_insert_policy` on `Space` (`rls_policy_always_true`). The insert policy is `WITH CHECK (true)`, but no client relies on it: `create-space` creates spaces with the service role. Whether to remove it is still open. Reading, changing and deleting a space still require access to it: those policies check `my_space_ids`.

### Performance advisor

These findings are expected:

## Function grants

A new function in `public` is executable by `authenticated` and `service_role`, not by `anon`. `base.sql` sets this with default privileges, in two parts:

- It revokes `anon` from the `public` schema's defaults, which Supabase sets up to include it.
- It revokes `PUBLIC` from the global defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it, so the first part alone changes nothing. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

Every `anon` grant and every revoke is explicit, next to the function in its schema file, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs it. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too.
input.new_string:
## Grants and default privileges

`base.sql` sets the default privileges of every object that `postgres` creates in `public`:

| Role            | Tables and views                   | Sequences         | Functions |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- | --------- |
| `anon`          | nothing                            | nothing           | nothing   |
| `authenticated` | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | `USAGE`, `SELECT` | `EXECUTE` |
| `service_role`  | everything                         | everything        | `EXECUTE` |

We set these ourselves because the Supabase image's defaults change between versions. Image 17.11.0.018 gives client roles only `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER` and `MAINTAIN` on new tables, and nothing on new sequences or functions, so a database built on it from migrations that relied on the image was unusable (ENG-2466).

Because `authenticated` can read and write a new table or view from the start:

- A new table must enable RLS. Without it, every signed-in user can read and write every row, in every space.
- A new view must run as the caller (`security_invoker`), or filter by the caller as the `my_*` views do. A definer view without such a filter shows every row to every signed-in user.

`base.sql` also revokes `PUBLIC` from the global function defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

The schema files declare only the exceptions to these defaults, next to the object, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs them: every `anon` grant, and every privilege removed from `authenticated` or `service_role`. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file. Don't write `GRANT ALL ... TO authenticated`: on a table, it includes `TRUNCATE`, which RLS doesn't limit.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its exceptions, such as an `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too. `REVOKE ALL ON TABLE` also removes the table's column grants, such as those on `PlatformAccount`.

input.old_string:
## Function grants

A new function in `public` is executable by `authenticated` and `service_role`, not by `anon`. `base.sql` sets this with default privileges, in two parts:

- It revokes `anon` from the `public` schema's defaults, which Supabase sets up to include it.
- It revokes `PUBLIC` from the global defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it, so the first part alone changes nothing. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

Every `anon` grant and every revoke is explicit, next to the function in its schema file, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs it. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too.
input.new_string:
## Grants and default privileges

`base.sql` sets the default privileges of every object that `postgres` creates in `public`:

| Role            | Tables and views                   | Sequences         | Functions |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- | --------- |
| `anon`          | nothing                            | nothing           | nothing   |
| `authenticated` | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | `USAGE`, `SELECT` | `EXECUTE` |
| `service_role`  | everything                         | everything        | `EXECUTE` |

We set these ourselves because the Supabase image's defaults change between versions. Image 17.11.0.018 gives client roles only `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER` and `MAINTAIN` on new tables, and nothing on new sequences or functions, so a database built on it from migrations that relied on the image was unusable (ENG-2466).

Because `authenticated` can read and write a new table or view from the start:

- A new table must enable RLS. Without it, every signed-in user can read and write every row, in every space.
- A new view must run as the caller (`security_invoker`), or filter by the caller as the `my_*` views do. A definer view without such a filter shows every row to every signed-in user.

`base.sql` also revokes `PUBLIC` from the global function defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

The schema files declare only the exceptions to these defaults, next to the object, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs them: every `anon` grant, and every privilege removed from `authenticated` or `service_role`. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file. Don't write `GRANT ALL ... TO authenticated`: on a table, it includes `TRUNCATE`, which RLS doesn't limit.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its exceptions, such as an `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too. `REVOKE ALL ON TABLE` also removes the table's column grants, such as those on `PlatformAccount`.

content.content:
# Designing cucumber tests

Cucumber is a harness for the gherkin language, allowing to make tests more legible. The steps are defined as regexp in `features/step-definitions/stepdefs.ts`. Currently, we assume the database is running with `turbo dev` in another terminal.

Some of test steps were defined to clear the database (`Given the database is blank`) or to put arbitrary data in the tables (`{word} are added to the database:`) which expects the name of a table as argument, and a markdown table for the table data.

The latter step requires some further explanations:

A lot of database objects use foreign keys, so we need to refer to numeric database identifiers. Those are defined by the database. To allow this to work, we have a pseudo-column called `$id`, which is a string alias that corresponds to the database numeric `id`. Make sure each value in that column is unique. We keep a dictionary of those aliases to the database numeric `id` in cucumber. When interpreting the table, if any other column is prefixed by a `_`, we will recursively search for strings and from the alias set and replace them with the appropriate database ids. Note that inserts are made in bulk, so you may need to break up your inserts according to dependencies. For example:

- Adding a schema first
  `And Concept are added to the database:`

  | $id | name | @is_schema |
  | alias1 | Claim | true |

- Then a concept referring to the schema
  `And Concept are added to the database:`
  | $id | name | @is_schema | \_schema_id |
  | alias2 | claim 1 | false | alias1 |

Also, cucumber treats all columns as strings; if they contain a non-string literal (essentially number, boolean or JSON) you can use the `@` prefix in the column name so the cell value will be parsed as json before sending to the database. (`@` comes before `_` if both are used.)

Other steps that require explanation:

- `a user logged in space {word} and calling getConcepts with these parameters: {string}`
- `Then query results should look like this`

This comes in pairs: The results from the query (whose parameters are defined as json) are checked against a table, using the same syntax as above. Only the columns defined are checked for equivalence.

- `the user {word} opens the {word} plugin in space {word}`.

This both creates the space and an account tied to that space. Because tying spaces and accounts goes through an edge function, it is the only good way to do both.
4

name: cucumber-run-recipe
description: How to run the database cucumber suite from the agent shell; three settings the shell lacks by default
metadata:

From `packages/database`, with `supabase_db_test` running (see [[never-run-cucumber-tests]]: ask first):

`PATH=/Users/maparent/.nvm/versions/node/v22.23.4/bin:$PATH SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID=test SUPABASE_USE_DB=local pnpm run test:withserve`

- `test:withserve` serves the edge functions (create-space) that "opens the plugin" needs; it refuses to run unless `SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID=test`.
- Reset the test DB with `SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID=test supabase db reset` (wipes it).
- Failures at the first step in every scenario mean environment, not the change under test.

     2. A DO loop over postgres-owned, non-extension relations in public (kinds r, p, v, m, S):

REVOKE ALL from authenticated on the 9 trigger-only functions: after_delete_space, after_delete_update_fref, after_insert_fref, concept_propagate_derived_columns, concept_set_derived_columns, is_last_local_reference(bigint, varchar), on_delete_local_reference, on_delete_space_revoke_local_access, on_update_local_reference.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/maparent/OpenSource/discourse-graph/.claude/skills/scope-check

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.

skills.name: dg-pr-adherence-check
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/maparent/OpenSource/discourse-graph/.claude/skills/dg-pr-adherence-check

# PR adherence check

Review the final change against the repository's current rules. Remain read-only unless the user authorizes fixes or PR updates. Do not post comments, request reviews, or change ticket status as part of this check.

## Resolve the evidence

1. Use the supplied PR or resolve the current branch's PR. Read its title, base and head commits, complete diff, body, checks, and review state. For local work, compare with the merge base of the intended PR base and include staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files. Identify unavailable metadata and explicitly exclude unrelated local work.
2. Read root `AGENTS.md`, `STYLE_GUIDE.md`, `PR_GUIDELINES.md`, and `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Read nested `AGENTS.md` files applicable to every changed path. Resolve these from the target repository, not the skill's installation directory. If reviewing changes to the rules themselves, also inspect the base versions so removing a requirement cannot silently erase a finding.
3. Resolve the Linear ticket from an explicit identifier, then the PR or branch. Use the repository's `$scope-check` skill for the `Done When` boundary and its separate Scope check output. Missing ticket access or acceptance criteria blocks the scope conclusion, not independent standards checks.
4. Use command results and manual testing evidence tied to the reviewed revision. A checked box or successful unrelated CI job is not proof of all validation. Record the reviewed head and any local changes so stale evidence is identifiable.

## Evaluate adherence

- Inspect the complete diff and enough surrounding code to assess applicable TypeScript, UI, organization, comments, documentation, hygiene, and testing rules. Focus findings on introduced or modified code, not unrelated existing debt.
- Check title and branch conventions, ticket linkage, PR body requirements, size guidance, split justification, review entry points, testing evidence, Loom, and review/check status against `PR_GUIDELINES.md`.
- Distinguish mandatory rules from preferences. Words such as “prefer” and “ideally,” the 200-line target, and the five-file guideline need judgment. Above 400 changed lines, excluding tests, check for the required explanation and review guide rather than rejecting the size alone.
- Explain concerns briefly to the PR author so they can address them; formal rule citations and evidence for each finding are not required. Do not invent exceptions, team approval, testing outcomes, or video contents. If a required document is unavailable or rules conflict without a clear applicable resolution, report the gap instead of guessing.
- Respect workflow timing: missing Loom or review evidence can be reported as outstanding before requesting review while a draft is being prepared. Do not call future post-merge steps violations on an open PR.
- Keep scope expansions in Scope check. Verification is optional. Standards check only records whether the check ran.

## Return the result

Return a copy-ready section:

```markdown
## Standards check

- [x] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.
```

The checkbox means the review ran, not that all requirements passed. If the diff cannot be resolved or the review could not run, leave it unchecked and tell the author what blocked it. Separately make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them; do not require these details in the PR body. Rerun affected checks after changes to code, rules, or PR metadata.

# DG Delegated Full Review

Use this skill only when the user invokes it directly or an explicitly requested workflow invokes it. Do not select it automatically.

Use `$dg-engineering-writing-style` when available. Look for it in the repository's `./.agents/skills` folder.

Run the review outside the primary agent's context. Do not modify files, fix findings, or delegate from the review subagent.

## Workflow reference

May be selected by `$*-run-scoped-engineering-workflow` at step 6 through its review dispatcher. Standalone use remains supported. This skill owns the single review subagent; never route back through the personal dispatcher. Preserve any caller-supplied acceptance boundary alongside the review target.

## Resolve the target

- Preserve a pull request, branch, commit, diff, or other review target supplied by the user.
- Otherwise, review all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes in the current working directory.
- If the working tree is clean, review the current branch against its merge base with the configured upstream or default base branch.

## Run the review

Create exactly one read-only subagent or task in the current working directory. Use the host-specific path that matches the available tools without asking the user which host is running:

- In Codex, spawn a subagent (not a new user-visible task) and direct it to run `/review` for the resolved target.
- In Claude Code, use an `Agent` subagent and direct it to run `/review`, the alias for `/code-review`. Use `/code-review` if the alias is unavailable.
- In another agent host, use its task or subagent mechanism and give the worker the natural-language review instructions below.

If the worker cannot invoke the slash command, have that same worker follow these instructions instead. Do not start a replacement worker or perform the review in the primary context.

```text
Perform a read-only, defect-first review of the requested code changes. Inspect the complete diff and enough surrounding code and tests to verify each issue. Report only concrete, actionable regressions introduced by the change. List findings by severity with precise file and line references. If there are no qualifying findings, return "No findings." Do not modify files or delegate the review.
```

Wait for the worker to finish. Return its findings to the primary conversation, preserving priorities and file references. If the worker fails, report the failure instead of completing the review inline.

## Close the review task

Capture the result before cleanup.

- In Codex, close the completed subagent when a non-destructive close or archive action is available. Otherwise report that the runtime does not support cleanup.
- Claude Code subagents are ephemeral and need no separate archive action.
- In another host, close or archive the completed task when a non-destructive lifecycle action is available.

Do not permanently delete a transcript or worktree as a substitute for closing or archiving it.

# DG Create Engineering Ticket

Create an Engineering ticket that another engineer can understand and implement without rediscovering its intent or scope.

Use `$dg-engineering-writing-style` when available. It is in the repository's `./.agents/skills` folder.

## Canonical template

The canonical Linear template is [General Engineering Task](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/new?template=6ca39698-3bce-449a-992e-059f0334e15b). Keep this link only as a reference in this skill. Never add it to a created ticket.

Use this exact template as the drafting checklist:

```markdown
## Problem

- What accepted user, developer, or project need does this address?
- Why does it need to be solved now?

## Solution

- What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

## Done When

- Describe how success is verified (behavioral or technical).
- Remember: Make only the smallest change needed to solve the problem.
- Remember: **Stay within the defined scope, or communicate any scope increase**

## Out of Scope

- (Optional) What adjacent cases, abstractions, or future work are explicitly not included?
- Link follow-up tickets where applicable

## Notes

- Additional Context, Blockers, dependencies, or follow-up actions.
```

Every bullet above is placeholder guidance. Replace or remove every placeholder before presenting a draft or creating a ticket. Keep all five headings, leaving `Out of Scope` or `Notes` empty when nothing useful applies. Use 1–3 short bullets per section unless the ticket is genuinely complex.

## Agent provenance and human review

Always use the Engineering team. This skill never creates or redirects to Feedback.

- Create every agent-created ticket in the existing `Ticket Draft` status with exactly one existing workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group. The label records provenance and stays after approval.
- Select the label from the creating agent's known identity: `Created by Claude` for Claude, `Created by Codex` for Codex, or `Created by LLM` for any other agent or when its identity cannot be determined. Do not infer agent identity from the Linear account, ticket topic, or skill name. Do not use `Created by LLM` as a substitute when the correct agent-specific label is missing.
- `Ticket Draft` is in the Backlog category and means human ticket review is pending; it does not authorize implementation. The existing `Draft` status belongs to the Started category and is used by the PR workflow. Do not use it for ticket review or change its automation.
- In `Notes`, record `Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket` and any other creation skills actually used. Skill attribution is provenance, not evidence that the ticket meets the standards.
- The human who asked the agent to create the ticket checks intent against the source request, scope and exclusions, verifiable acceptance criteria, and the canonical template and engineering writing standards. Keep the ticket in `Ticket Draft` while changes are needed.
- Human approval moves the ticket to `Backlog` when the problem and fix are agreed and implementation needs no further product or solution decisions. Use `Triage` when implementation is likely within six months but decisions remain. Keep idea-stage Engineering requests in Engineering.
- The human's move from `Ticket Draft` to `Triage` or `Backlog` records sign-off. An agent may make that move only after explicit human approval of the completed ticket and destination. A request to create a ticket is not approval of its generated contents. Keep the provenance label and skill attribution.

## Project selection

Resolve the project in this order:

1. Use the project explicitly named by the user.
2. Use a clearly relevant active project from the current work context.
3. For Obsidian work with no relevant project, leave the project empty and apply the existing `Obsidian plugin` label. Do not use `Obsidian Discourse Graphs plugin assorted tasks`; the Obsidian queue picks up unprojected issues by label (see DIS-617).
4. For Roam work, use `Roam Discourse Graph plugin assorted tasks`.
5. Otherwise, use `Engineering Ops assorted tasks`.

Any project you select must exist, not be completed, canceled, archived, or trashed, and include the Engineering team. Never create a project. If a user-specified project is missing, ambiguous, or inactive, ask the user for another project instead of silently substituting one. Obsidian tickets that do belong to a real project still use that project, plus the `Obsidian plugin` label.

## Labels and optional fields

- Inspect existing issue labels and apply every clearly relevant label. Always apply `Obsidian plugin` to Obsidian work, since it is how unprojected Obsidian tickets reach the queue.
- Never create a label or guess an uncertain label.
- Missing or uncertain optional labels do not block creation. If `Ticket Draft`, the required provenance label, or `Obsidian plugin` for Obsidian work is missing or ambiguous, return the prepared draft and report the configuration gap instead of creating an unmarked ticket or substituting a status.
- Set priority only when the user or context makes it clear and useful.
- Do not set a cycle or release. CI/CD handles releases.

## Create or draft

Draft without changing Linear when the user asks for a draft, review, or rewrite. Create the ticket without an additional confirmation when the user explicitly asks to create it.

Before creation, resolve the current Engineering statuses, selected project, and existing labels. Create the issue once with its title, completed description (including skill attribution), `Ticket Draft` status, project (omitted for unprojected Obsidian work), provenance and relevant labels, and justified priority. If the result is ambiguous, search for the issue before retrying so a transient failure does not create a duplicate.

Read the created issue back and verify its status, labels, and attribution. For unprojected Obsidian work, confirm the project is empty and `Obsidian plugin` is applied. Report any mismatch instead of claiming successful routing. Return the issue identifier, title, status, project, and link, and say that human review is pending. Include the generated branch name when Linear returns one. Do not restate the full description unless the user asks.
